content: The quality of education provided by public or government educational sectors in lowand middle-income countries shows significant disparities between urban and rural areas. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized that implementing day-care programs in rural regions of these countries could help address this inequity and positively influence early childhood development for children in traditionally underserved areas. The guideline development process revealed numerous research gaps, highlighting the need for additional data to optimize drowning prevention interventions in lowand middle-income countries. For programs such as day-care services, basic swimming skills, and water safety training, there is a critical need for more robust data collection and peer-reviewed publications. Organizations and regions undertaking these initiatives are strongly encouraged to gather and publish data throughout the implementation process. Key outcomes to evaluate include drowning-related mortality and morbidity, improvements in children’s swimming and water safety skills, program cost-effectiveness, and safety-related incidents. National governments and stakeholders developing new programs for children should integrate research and evaluation components to refine future projects. For regions with existing programs, an evaluative framework should be implemented to assess feasibility and address research gaps. Sharing data through open-access platforms and academic literature is essential for successful global implementation. The World Health Organization (WHO) will leverage its networks and resources to promote awareness and understanding of these guidelines through international conferences, its website, news releases, and technical support. At the practical level, WHO and its partners have been collaborating with national and subnational governments to address drowning in high-burden settings. Community involvement is critical at all stages of implementation, including conducting epidemiological surveys, identifying drowning risk factors, and discussing traditional responses to drowning incidents. Sociocultural factors that may hinder implementation must be addressed to ensure programs are feasible and acceptable to the target population. WHO recommends conducting a comprehensive situation assessment to evaluate the likelihood of sustainable, equitable, and effective community involvement before implementing interventions. This assessment should be carried out in collaboration with local partners, such as government agencies, parent groups, community leaders, and relevant NGOs. Social autopsy methods have proven effective in engaging communities in discussions about drowning risk factors and raising awareness about prevention programs. Community surveys to determine the incidence and risk factors for drowning can provide detailed etiological information to inform targeted interventions. Research priorities outlined in the guideline should be strongly considered by all partners, as implementing these interventions offers an opportunity to contribute to peer-reviewed knowledge in this field. The guideline development process adhered to standard WHO procedures, involving planning discussions, collaboration with the Guideline Review Committee Secretariat, and engagement of an experienced GRADE methodologist. A Guideline Development Group, WHO Steering Group, and External Review Group were established, ensuring technical expertise, geographical representation, and gender balance. Declarations of interest and confidentiality agreements were secured, and biographies of GDG members were made publicly available. The evidence review process involved developing and refining PICO questions with input from the evidence review team, WHO, and the methodologist. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, GDG briefings and panel meetings were conducted remotely, utilizing tools like Panel Voice for evidence review data and pre-voting on EtD framework questions. The conclusions were synthesized into the final guideline, which underwent further refinement by the GDG, WHO Steering Group, and External Review Group before submission to the Guideline Review Committee.
